title: One Reason for Each Team to Be Thankful This Season
contentHtml:
It’s Thanksgiving week, and I’m free to do whatever I want here—including using the “let’s give thanks for something” gimmick to bounce around the entire NBA.

Here’s one thing each of the league’s 30 teams (and their fan bases) can be thankful for this week.

Atlanta Hawks

That so many teams did not realize what they had in Nickeil Alexander-Walker. The New Orleans Pelicans drafted Alexander-Walker at no. 17 in 2019—after trading the no. 4 pick (which became De’Andre Hunter) to the Atlanta Hawks for nos. 8, 17, and 35.

(The Pelicans had acquired the no. 4 pick from the Los Angeles Lakers in the Anthony Davis deal, which will finally wind to its conclusion when the Pelicans trade Dejounte Murray. New Orleans nailed the initial Davis deal and then botched almost every follow-up transaction, including by flipping two of the key assets to Atlanta—Dyson Daniels and two first-round picks—for Murray. The Pelicans may want to just stop trading with the Hawks. Maybe two avian teams should not be able to make trades without league approval.)

Alexander-Walker didn’t make a dent in New Orleans over two-plus seasons before the Pels tossed him in almost as an afterthought to the deal that sent Josh Hart—another part of the Davis bounty—and draft assets to the Portland Trail Blazers for CJ McCollum. The McCollum experience went fine for New Orleans until it inexplicably traded him for Jordan Poole (and Saddiq Bey, to be fair) on a longer contract. McCollum, of course, is now on the Hawks.

The Blazers had Alexander-Walker for one day before they semi-salary-dumped him to the Utah Jazz for Joe Ingles (on an expiring contract). One unremarkable year later, Utah sent Alexander-Walker to the Minnesota Timberwolves in a three-way deal in which the Jazz targeted a Lakers first-rounder in exchange for absorbing Russell Westbrook’s salary.

Alexander-Walker popped in Minnesota. The Wolves knew exactly what they had when Alexander-Walker hit free agency in July 2025; in navigating a salary crunch, they chose to retain Naz Reid over him.

Now, Alexander-Walker is the leading scorer on perhaps the league’s most interesting and funky team—a feisty defender who bombs 3s of all stripes and might deserve a back-end All-Star spot. Alexander-Walker plays hard, and he plays to win. He’s one of my very favorite players.

Boston Celtics

That Neemias Queta is a representative starting center—and that the Kings, shockingly, waived him before even beginning to tap into his potential.

The Celtics are in a rut—and perhaps nearing a crossroads of sorts—but they’d be much worse off without Queta holding the fort on both ends. Mitchell Robinson has been a nonfactor, and Luka Garza—while productive—has a minutes-per-game shelf life on a good team.

Queta is a solid defender, a voracious rebounder, and more of an all-around threat on offense than the Celtics had probably envisioned—even if some of his one-dribble takes can be perilous. (Queta appears to stumble amid crowds of defenders but then somehow rights himself, and one of his giant extend-o arms emerges from the chaos to flip the ball toward the rim.)

He’s 5-of-7 on 3s and dishing about three dimes per 36 minutes—including some snazzy passes out of the pick-and-roll:

That’s a rare make for Derrick White these days. I don’t want to talk about it.

Brooklyn Nets

That not many people really care about the Nets in the wake of the Knicks’ title run, or realize that Brookyn’s first-round pick in yet another tanktastic season is heading to the Houston Rockets?

Nolan Traore is really the only feel-good story of another lost season, and now he’s out at least two months with a hamstring strain. Does anyone know where Ben Saraf is? Is Egor Demin ready to play more on the ball again? Can the Nets just make Mikel Brown Jr. their Darius Acuff Jr.—give him the keys and let him do anything he wants? Brown is an electric athlete who changes speeds and directions in a blink. He is a bewildered mess on defense, but in the kind of bewildered and messy way that is expected for a rookie.

Charlotte Hornets

That rebounding remains important, and that they have Moussa Diabaté to do it.

Charlotte is averaging 104 points per 100 possessions—dead last by a mile, nearly three points behind Utah’s no. 29–ranked fart factory. Imagine how bad Charlotte would be if it didn’t rank no. 1 in offensive rebounding! It tops the league in defensive rebounding, too! The Hornets are a rebounding juggernaut!

Someone needs to study how Charles Lee has created this rebounding machine because this doesn’t look on paper—or in physical stature—like an elite rebounding team. Diabaté is their best rebounder, but Charlotte is about as airtight on the glass when he’s on the bench.

But man, is Diabaté a monster. He knows what will get him paid in (unrestricted!) free agency this summer, and he wants the damned ball more than you. He is a pointy-elbowed agitator who will crack anyone in the ribs, and he will get right in your face if you object to his tactics.

Diabaté leads the league in offensive rebounds and has recovered 19 percent of Charlotte’s misses. Only six players have ever recorded a single-season offensive rebounding rate above 19 percent, according to Basketball-Reference. (Moses Malone did it three times, while Dennis Rodman and Jayson Williams did it twice apiece.)

Chicago Bulls

That they have Caleb Wilson, and that draftniks consider the upcoming draft class so meh that many are wondering whether the (somewhat accidental) benefits of being in the relegation zone might outweigh the reduced odds of picking near the top. Remember: New anti-tanking rules stipulate that no team can pick no. 1 two years in a row or in the top five for three consecutive drafts. Perhaps having slightly lower chances of nabbing the no. 1 pick this season is not the worst thing for the Bulls—one of the relegation-zone teams that controls its first-round pick.

Also, Tre Jones is awesome and somehow the most important thing Chicago got back in the Zach LaVine and DeMar DeRozan trades combined. (The San Antonio Spurs received the real goods in both deals by acting as a third-party broker—i.e., a smart franchise preying on the weak. Cruel stuff.)

Teams in need of a super-high-quality backup point guard are already calling Chicago about Jones, sources say. Sixty percent of Jones’s shot attempts come in the restricted area. That is the shot profile of a center!
